captions.text: Imagine you own a bike shop. A customer is coming back this afternoon, and her bike still needs brake pads.
You’re under another bike. So you let your purchasing agent order a box from one of your regular suppliers.
Across town, the supplier has the parts packed. An order came from the agent, but there’s one question before the box leaves the dock.
Did the shop owner actually give the agent permission to buy this?
Let’s test that question. We changed the supplier on a twenty-dollar test order. The agent signed it anyway.
Will it go through? First, look at the permission the owner actually signed.
The owner signs a mandate with a hundred dollars of test budget and two approved suppliers.
The agent can authorize up to twenty-five dollars alone. Above that, a second person must sign the same request.
We gave a local language model two tools: read the mandate, and submit an invoice.
It declined supplier C. In a separate run, it submitted twenty dollars for supplier A, and the ledger accepted.
Now follow one recorded mandate from start to finish. First, the agent asks for twenty dollars for supplier A.
The checks pass. The budget falls from a hundred dollars to eighty.
Then the agent signs for the same amount, payable to someone else. This is our simulated compromised agent.
We replayed all eight rules against the recorded request. Seven passed. The supplier check failed.
The ledger recorded the refusal. Eighty dollars remained.
What if a stranger names the right supplier? The signing key is wrong. The budget holds.
Next comes a forty-dollar invoice. With just the agent’s signature, the ledger refuses it.
The designated second signer signs the very same request. Now the request goes through, and forty dollars remain.
The owner revokes the mandate. Even a fresh ten-dollar request for an approved supplier fails.
Back at the shipping desk, the supplier can check the forty-dollar order. First, verify both signatures on that request.
Then follow the record through its proof to the pinned snapshot. It shows the authorization, and a later record shows the revocation.
Change the saved balance by one cent. The record no longer matches its proof, and the verifier rejects it.
The supplier can now see which order the shop authorized and when that permission ended.
This demo used one local snapshot source. Independent validator quorum verification is still open.
The signed request and both checkpoints are in the repository. You can replay the decision yourself.
